cards.title: Positioning: turn a commodity into a category of one
cards.summary: Reframe your store from a generic product category into a distinctive, ownable identity so you stop blending in with competitors.
cards.use_when: You are writing your homepage headline, brand tagline, or About/positioning statement for a store that currently describes itself generically (e.g. 'quality home goods store').
steps: Replace generic category labels with a specific identity that implies a method, specialization, or system. Source examples: not 'office cleaner' but 'Office Cleaning Technicians'; not 'real estate office' but 'Experts of the RapidSell System'.

If the higher positioning doesn't exist yet, build a program or process and name it, then make it real (your stated identity must match actual operations). The source explicitly warns that saying you're an expert doesn't make you one.
Align the whole store experience to the claim: operations, supplier quality, packaging, support tone, and imagery must be congruent or word-of-mouth will expose the gap and the positioning will fail.
Audit every generic competitor phrase on your site and replace it with a specific, verifiable version of what you do differently.
caveats: The source insists the product/service must be genuinely excellent first, otherwise you 'educate your buyer away' from you.
Positioning is only as strong as the operational backing; promising 'technicians' while delivering untrained service backfires.

cards.title: Make your ad hook 'specifically unique' instead of vague
cards.summary: Use concrete, specific, unexpected hooks instead of generic category claims to earn more readership and clicks.
cards.use_when: You are drafting ad creative or a product landing page headline in a crowded category where every competitor uses the same generic promise.
steps: Compare a generic headline ('Work from Home and Turn Your Email Into Big Profits') against a specific one ('19-Year Old College Kid Discovers Clever Way to Persuade People to Send You Money Via PayPal'). The source argues the specific one wins because it paints a clear mental picture.
Ask yourself: what's unique about my offer, my process, my product? Can I be the only one claiming this? Is there something unique about me I can leverage?

Use real, truthful specifics from your own operations (your size, your story, your method). The source gives examples like 'Big Bald Chris Teaches Wing Chun' and '6'5", 275-Pound Man Offers the BIGGEST Computer Discounts'—each is honest but vivid.
Back the distinctiveness with matching imagery (e.g. hire a photographer to emphasize the real attribute, like shooting from floor level to emphasize size).
caveats: Stay truthful—'find an intriguing way to say it' does not mean fabricate claims.
The source cites Starch Research that fresh/new headlines deliver higher 'Read Most' scores, but that is the source's cited finding, not your store's data.

cards.title: Build an authority position and make content as the evidence
cards.summary: Become the recognized expert in your niche by publishing knowledge in many formats, which lowers buyer skepticism and builds trust before purchase.
cards.use_when: You want your store to be seen as the go-to expert in a niche, and you need to convert expertise into a concrete content and trust-building plan.
steps: Whoever writes your marketing must first regard their knowledge as valuable—the source defines this mindset shift as Step 1 of authority positioning.
Get a professional headshot in appropriate attire and put it on product pages, ads, emails, brochures, contracts—everywhere.

Publish short reports (the source suggests 3–10 pages, PDF and hardcopy) with your headshot and business name on the cover, e.g. 'How to Use 10 Little-Known Printing Secrets to Make Your Business Look More Professional'.

Run editorial-style Q&A 'columns' (3 short questions with short answers, headshot at top, business name/address/phone at bottom) in local papers—sometimes these are accepted free if they offer useful info.
Run free clinics/workshops with samples that teach the buyer how to judge quality, then let your offer do the selling.
Offer the reports as free lead magnets to anyone who comes in or registers.
caveats: The source's printer case study is one person's result; replicate the method, not a promised number.
Claims of authority must be backed by real demonstrated knowledge; the source explicitly states to assume 'excellent grasp on your subject' before adopting an authority stance.

cards.title: Use a customer survey as a sales letter in disguise
cards.summary: Mail a short survey with an exclusive thank-you offer embedded to collect buyer insight and generate an easy incremental sale.
cards.use_when: You want to know what customers actually think and, at the same time, drive a repeat purchase or upgrade with minimal friction.
steps: Write a short personal letter (8.5x11 stationery) asking 5–6 questions about satisfaction, price perception, and likelihood to re-buy, using 1–10 scales for easy completion.
Add one open-ended question to surface free feedback, e.g. 'If you were the owner of my business, what would you do differently?'
At the end, embed an offer you would have offered anyway, framed as an exclusive thank-you only for survey respondents (e.g. a 50% off product, free consultation, or voucher).
Include a YES block and payment/confirmation mechanic so respondents can return payment with the survey, e.g. 'a $10 product for just $5—postage paid—only for survey respondents'.
Use mail-merge to make the letter look personal, not mass-produced.
Offer a free thank-you for taking the survey (e.g. a free slice) and limit response time to keep costs controlled.
caveats: The source claims this is effective for a wide range of businesses but warns the offer must feel like an exclusive thank-you, not a standard promo.
Feedback can be more valuable than the extra sales profit, but the survey response rate depends on list quality and ease of reply.

cards.title: Format a survey for maximum response
cards.summary: Use a double postcard or one-page letter with a postage-paid reply envelope and mostly multiple-choice questions to maximize survey returns.
cards.use_when: You are physically mailing survey cards or letters to your customers and need the highest possible reply rate to make the feedback useful.
steps: Choose a format: a double postcard split by a perforation (one side addressed to recipient, the other is the survey card) OR a one-page 8.5x11 letter with a survey and stamp-free reply envelope.
Use a Business Reply Mail permit indicia on the reply card so respondents don't need a stamp; the source states ease is the secret of good survey response.
Keep everything short—ideally letter and survey fit on one page (front, both sides if needed)—to reduce handling and confusion.
Use semantic differential scales (1–10) for all questions where possible, e.g. 'On a scale 1 to 10, how likely are you to return to us within two weeks?'
Bribe respondents with a free item (e.g. free slice) but limit the response window to keep costs and logistics under control.
caveats: The source stresses the personal letter/envelope format gets more attention, but it means more manual processing than a digital survey.
The free reward and postage-paid reply are real costs that must be weighed against the value of the feedback.

cards.title: Use 'grabbers' to force attention on your direct mail or package inserts
cards.summary: Attach a small physical object to your mailer or insert to create curiosity and a sense of obligation to read your offer.
cards.use_when: You send physical mail to prospects or include marketing inserts in shipments and need something that makes your piece stand out in the stack.
steps: Attach a small, relevant object to the top of the letter or insert (penny, dollar bill, sand baggy, chocolate wrapper, poorly printed sample) that relates to your offer.

Open with copy that names the grabber and immediately ties it to the promise, e.g. 'As you can see, I have attached a crisp one-dollar bill...I'll show you how to save 100 of these when you buy carpet'.
Match the grabber to your category: real estate—baggy of sand; collection agency—an NSF check; candy shop—a wrapper with a coupon for a free sample; printer—a poorly printed brochure.
Test with an A/B split: mail 500 letters with the grabber vs. 500 without, and compare response.
Ensure the grabber won't rip the envelope or create postal handling problems—consider bubble-wrap-lined envelopes for bulky items.
caveats: The source says the technique worked for Robert Collier in 1937 and should be tested; it is not a guarantee.
A grabber that is too bulky or sharp may damage the mail piece or get flagged by postal carriers.

cards.title: Long copy outsells short copy—if you keep it interesting
cards.summary: Well-written long copy beats short copy because it satisfies both detail-hungry buyers and quick deciders, online and offline.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how much copy a sales page, product page, or email should carry, especially in a high-consideration purchase.
steps: Write enough to inform, build desire, convince, and motivate—restating benefits from several different angles and perspectives (e.g. how the customer will feel, how others will see them, how safe/practical it is).
Address both emotional and logical appeals so you speak to both peripheral and central-route thinkers (car ads are the source's model: status, safety, economy).
Pile on benefits, testimonials, and a warranty—the source calls this stacking social proof and fear-reduction.
Accept that some buyers decide after the headline, so long copy doesn't hurt them; it only gives more-information buyers what they need.
Don't pad—Gary Halbert's cited line is 'Copy can never be too long, only too boring.'
caveats: The source cites Ogilvy, Caples, Hopkins, and MarketingExperiments.com, and a single Online-Learning.com case where quadrupling homepage copy was associated with ~20% more enrollments—these are examples, not guarantees.
The source's claim is aggressive ('long copy invariably outsells short copy'), but the necessary condition is well-written, relevant copy—short copy is only right when there is little to say.

cards.title: Make your ad look like editorial content to lift readership
cards.summary: Camouflage ads in the typeface, column width, and news voice of the publication so more readers stop and read.
cards.use_when: You place ads in newspapers, newsletters, or niche publications where ad blindness is high and you want higher readership.
steps: Write the ad as a news story: same typeface, column width, and leading as the surrounding articles, headline included.
Open with a news-style lead, e.g. 'Local Hypnotist Announces New Way to Quit Smoking in 48 Hours'.
Use reporter voice and work in customer quotes—e.g. 'I thought I'd never quit, said Scott Lawrence, one of Halshire's successful patients.'
Keep tone objective; the source explicitly warns never to sound too enthusiastic or 'hypey' or you blow the camouflage effect.
Read a few actual news stories from that publication before writing to match the tone.
End with a low-friction call to action, e.g. offer a free report by phone or website.
caveats: Readership lift estimates in the source vary widely: Ogilvy claimed 50% better readership, Caples 80%, Richard Benson 500–600%—treat as source-cited figures, not benchmarks.
Camouflage only works if the writer can genuinely mimic editorial voice; a hypey ad in news clothing reads as deceptive.

cards.title: Wrap important offers in a coupon border to trigger savings associations
cards.summary: Surround an order form, bonus, or reply device with a broken coupon-style border to leverage conditioned 'savings' associations.
cards.use_when: You are designing order forms, bonus boxes, or reply coupons on a landing page, print ad, or email and want to increase response.
steps: Draw a bold, broken block-type border around the offer, order form, flyer, or reply coupon. The source reports success wrapping bonus copy in a 3-point coupon border with a light yellow tint.
Use it whether or not the piece is an actual money-off coupon—the source claims even non-money-off coupons lift response because of conditioning.
Make the border visually coupon-like, e.g. rectangles as the border 'dots' instead of circles.
Keep coupon borders on the offer block only, not the entire page, to preserve its specificity.
Test coupon-bordered vs. unbordered versions of the same offer.
caveats: The source cites Coupon Council and CMS/PMA data showing high coupon use across income and age groups; these are U.S. market stats from the book's era, so verify current relevance.
The mechanism is explained via anchoring/classical conditioning, which is the source's framing—treat it as a hypothesis to test, not proven causation for your store.

cards.title: Match images to product and use them to demonstrate
cards.summary: Show the product in use, with people and context, to lift readership and clicks over plain product or no-image ads.
cards.use_when: You are choosing hero images and creative for product pages, ads, or landing pages and want to maximize attention and relevance.
steps: Show the product rather than omitting it—the source cites a 13% readership lift vs. showing no product.

Prefer product-in-use shots over product-only shots; the source cites a further 13% boost from adding action/drama/context (e.g. pepper spray illustrated stopping attackers vs. a hand holding the can).
Include people: photos or illustrations with people lift 'noted' scores by about 25% over no people in the cited research.
Give photos context—e.g. a refrigerator in a working kitchen rather than a studio background (Starch Research guidance).

Use these high-attention image types, ranked by the source's Gallup/Parade findings: (1) children/babies, (2) mothers and babies, (3) groups of adults/people, (4) animals, (5) sports scenes, (6) celebrities, (7) food.
caveats: The source cites a 1991 Roper Starch study of 2,000 consumers and 650 newspaper ads and a Gallup/Kimberly-Clark Sunday-newspaper survey—historic print-media research; results are examples, not promises for online contexts.
The source emphasizes pictures only influence brand choice if there's a clear connection to the brand and message; gratuitous imagery can hurt.

cards.title: Use visual density and large formats to lift ad readership
cards.summary: Ads with more visual elements and larger formats get seen and read more than sparse or standard-sized ads.
cards.use_when: You are planning ad layout, banner sizing, or the visual-to-text ratio of a paid placement and want to boost noted/read-most metrics.
steps: Aim for visuals to occupy roughly 50–75% of the ad; the source cites 30% higher 'Noted' at 50% visuals and 50% higher at 75% visuals vs. ads with little or no visuals.
Include multiple visuals: 4–9 visuals lift 'Noted' by ~30%, and 10+ visuals are ~55% more likely to be Noted with 'Read Most' up ~70% (source-cited Roper Starch figures).

For online banners, use 'skyscraper' (tall vertical) and 'leaderboard' (large banner) formats rather than standard-size banners—larger ads outperform smaller ones according to C-NET research cited by the source.
Prefer interactive (DHTML) ads over static where supported.

If using a print half-page, specify a 'Half-Page Island' (two columns wide, three-quarters page deep) so the newspaper can't pack other ads around yours; the source reports papers often place only news next to such ads.
caveats: All numeric lifts are source-cited historic print/C-NET research; verify current ad platform behavior before relying on them.
The 'Length-Implies-Strength' effect (big ads perceived as more successful) is the source's framing, not a proven purchase driver.

cards.title: Test offers systematically, not just copy
cards.summary: If ads or pages underperform, revise the offer itself—framing, free extras, and segmentation—before abandoning the product.
cards.use_when: Your ad, product page, or email is underperforming and you have already tried headline changes but response is still weak.
steps: Change the offer rather than the headline first when the current ad is simply 'announcing' the business, e.g. a Grand Opening announcement offers nothing; replace it with a free spinal evaluation or 50% off first visit.
Try framing the same discount differently: 'Buy One Get One FREE' is reported by the source to outperform '50% off' because 'free' is a stronger word.
Segment the offer: 'FREE Spinal Exams for Runners' one month, 'for Body Builders' the next—keep rotating to find the resonant audience.
Add a bonus the customer wants and can be delivered cheaply, e.g. a free massage with every visit (source suggests using a massage school student).
Test structural variations: family special, husband-and-wife deal, senior rate, every-fifth-visit-free, or an authoritative report as a lead-magnet offer.
caveats: The source insists the marketplace, not you, tells you what works—if the phone doesn't ring or coupons aren't redeemed, that is the feedback.
Extreme offers (e.g. an oversized novelty gift) may 'bomb or take your practice in a whole new direction'—which is why you test rather than assume.
Price is also a variable—if the offer change doesn't work, check whether you are simply out of line with the market.

cards.title: Ask the market before you build the promo
cards.summary: Survey your target market before spending on campaigns so you build around what they actually want, not what you assume.
cards.use_when: You are about to invest in a major promotion, new product launch, or seasonal campaign and want to de-risk it with research.
steps: Define the target market and find a way to reach them (source example: everyone within a 5-mile radius of a pizzeria, or your own customer list).
Ask direct questions: what do you like, dislike, prefer, want more of, what's your biggest complaint, what would make you come more often, what's the most you'd pay for a specific product?
Offer a small incentive (e.g. a free slice) to take the survey, and set a short response window to control costs.
Use the answers to shape the offer, price, and copy of the campaign—the source argues this is cheaper than guessing with thousands in ads.
Confirm the buyer's world before selling: the source's bottled-water example—selling door-to-door in a city where everyone has a well—shows the cost of skipping this step.
caveats: The source claims agencies must research before creative and that competitors rarely do it—this is a competitive advantage argument, not a proven universal.
Survey results reflect what respondents say, not necessarily what they buy; keep the survey data as strong input, not a guarantee.

cards.title: Use editorial and survey assets again and again
cards.summary: Repetition and multi-format reuse of proven assets overcome the fact that any one insertion reaches only a fraction of your audience.
cards.use_when: You are planning media frequency or content repurposing and wonder whether to keep running a proven ad or asset.
steps: Plan to run a proven ad or campaign repeatedly—the source notes ad agencies re-run commercials because any single exposure captures only a fraction of attention.
Repurpose one asset across formats: a report becomes an ad, a lead magnet, a workshop handout, and a follow-up.
For print, don't place one ad once and assume the job is done—only a certain percentage of readers read any single insertion.

For online, keep sending a recurring, well-segmented email to your list; the source reports surveys from Forrester Research and NFO World Group in which ~31–35% of recipients preferred one mailing per week.
Track which asset continues to outperform and rotate rather than replace.
caveats: The frequency stats cited are the source's cited survey findings; your list's preferences may differ—segment to find out.
Repetition without relevance or variation becomes fatigue; the source warns against rambling and against copy that's boring.

cards.title: 7 online response boosters and their traps
cards.summary: Use email frequency, HTML vs. text, subject lines, ad format, animation, and specificity to lift online response—without confusing clicks for sales.
cards.use_when: You are designing an email campaign or banner ads and need concrete online response guidance rather than print-era assumptions.
steps: Email cadence: the source cites surveys showing a plurality of recipients (~31–35%) prefer one email per week; test cadence against your own list rather than assuming daily is best.
Format: the source reports HTML generated ~200% better response than plain text (Jupiter Research) but some users block HTML—run an A/B split of HTML vs. text to your own list before committing.

Subject lines and sender: maximize open rate with a familiar sender name, a personal subject line including the recipient's name, and a precision-targeted offer (source reports 60%+ open as excellent for opt-in B2B ezines).
Ad format: skyscrapers and leaderboards outperform standard banner sizes; large beats small; interactive (DHTML) beats non-interactive (C-NET study cited).
Animation: animated ads are cited as at least 15% and up to 40% better on click-through than static—but keep motion relevant and avoid rapid flashing.

Specificity over mystery: the source says mystery/cryptic ads can lift click-through ~18% but convert poorly because of poor targeting. Use an honest, specific subject line like 'Need a Low-Interest Mortgage?'
caveats: The source warns to never confuse clicks with sales; high click-through from a mystery hook is often wasted traffic.
Click-through rate depends heavily on list quality—source reports anything from under 1% on poorly crafted rented-list offers to over 20% for strong offers to your own customers.

cards.title: Position yourself before you position the product
cards.summary: Business positioning and offer positioning are two different jobs—do the business identity first, then customize each campaign's offer positioning.
cards.use_when: You are splitting time between building a brand identity and writing individual campaign or product offers and need to keep the two distinct.
steps: Separate (a) your business identity/authority position from (b) the specific offer positioning in any given ad or page.
For business positioning: claim a distinctive identity, back it with operations, imagery, published knowledge, and repetition.
For offer positioning: in a crowded category (source uses late-night 'make money' infomercials as the example), pick a hook that is specifically unique and truthful rather than another vague promise.
Read Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind for a step-by-step process to build your image based on where you are now and where you want to be.
Regularly audit: if a competitor is saying what you're saying, change either the claim or the proof that backs it.
caveats: The source ties the business position to actual capability, warning that a strong tagline without substance collapses under word-of-mouth.
Offer positioning changes should be tested, not assumed—the marketplace decides which framing wins.

What I say I am and how I’m perceived are now congruent. This is how you make your business fit your new positioning. Late-night infomercials that claim to teach you how to make gobs of cash are more prolific than tech nerds at a PC convention. This is where great positioning is really needed for your ads to stand out. For example, which of these two headlines attracts your attention most? Tip: If you want your ad to stand out from the crowd, say something different. Create ads that are different and instantly recognizable. The point is to create a hook (or positioning) that’s different from what thousands of other advertisers are saying. Be truthful, but find an intriguing way to say it! When you use this idea, you’re taking advantage of what’s called an anchor in neuro-linguistic programming (NLP). An anchor is a conditioned response that’s set off by the introduction of a particular stimulus. Russian scientist Ivan Pavlov rang the bell and fed the dog, rang the bell and fed the dog, rang the bell and fed the dog. Soon, after all these repetitions, he was able to make the dog drool by simply ringing the bell. The bell was the anchor. A link between the bell and the food was made in the dog’s brain, and a “conditioned reflex”—copious drooling—resulted. To the dog, the bell actually meant food.
